talk_track: I help independent school boards answer the technology-risk questions their leadership teams can't -- cybersecurity, AI use, and vendor accountability -- without displacing the IT vendors already in place. Your open Chief of Business Operations role puts one person in charge of "the day-to-day management of Facilities, Information Technology, and Administrative Services," reporting to the Integrator. The read most schools miss: when IT lives inside a facilities-and-admin portfolio, you get solid help-desk coverage and no governance layer -- nobody whose job is telling the board what the vendors are actually doing with student and family data. That lands differently at St. Philip's than at a tuition-driven school, because contributions were roughly two-thirds of your $15.6M in FY2024, so donor confidence is what a mishandled vendor incident really costs. Whoever you hire will own the plumbing; the board still needs someone to translate it. Worth a note on what that gap usually looks like?
caveats: Enrollment (~250 PK-8 students, per privateschoolreview 2026 and the school's own FY2023 990 program description of 265 children) sits well below Kenneth's stated 800-2,000 band. It clears the intent of that band on every other axis -- $12.0M annual expenses, 138 employees, a 25-member board of trustees, and a school + community center + neighborhood-development footprint -- but the headcount mismatch is real and unresolved.

Kenneth's tuition-attrition EDP does not map here. St. Philip's serves low- and moderate-income families and drew $10.56M of its $15.59M FY2024 revenue from contributions, so the analogous existential number is donor confidence, not tuition churn. The talk track reflects that substitution.
No IT director or technology leader appears in any public org chart or leadership page; absence of evidence, not confirmed absence.
